evidence.claim: Reuters reported that Elvira Nabiullina resisted calls from powerful industrialists and the Economy Ministry for interest-rate cuts, and a cited economist said she must have had Putin's support to do this.
evidence.title: Tough choices ahead for Russia's inflation hawk Nabiullina
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that Elvira Nabiullina resisted calls from powerful industrialists and the Economy Ministry for interest-rate cuts, and a cited economist said she must have had Putin's support to do this.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters contemporaneous reporting with named officials and quoted market participants; still mediated reporting, not a direct state record.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year 2022; early-war monetary-policy choice and ruler support signal within the period.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect but meaningful: the article ties Nabiullina's technocratic stance to Putin's support, which is relevant to whether he empowered competent economic professionals.
contrary_evidence: The central bank is institutionally independent, so this does not prove detailed Putin authorship of each policy move.
Some of the stability came from emergency macro measures and the shock itself, not broad prosperity policy.

evidence.claim: Putin proposed nominating Elvira Nabiullina for a third term in a bid to ensure macroeconomic stability, and Reuters noted she was a committed inflation fighter resisting pressure for rate cuts.
evidence.title: Putin tips central bank chief Nabiullina for third term to ensure economic stability
evidence.excerpt: Putin proposed nominating Elvira Nabiullina for a third term in a bid to ensure macroeconomic stability, and Reuters noted she was a committed inflation fighter resisting pressure for rate cuts.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters contemporaneous report based on a Kremlin spokesman and clear attribution of the nomination proposal.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year 2022; direct personnel decision during the sanctions shock.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct on the nomination proposal; partially indirect on monetary-policy empowerment because the central bank sets rates independently, but Putin's retention choice mattered.
contrary_evidence: The Bank of Russia still acted as an institution with some independence.
This says little about whether the broader economic agenda favored broad-based prosperity.

evidence.claim: Nabiullina said the urgent measures taken after the early-2022 sanctions shock helped prevent an inflationary spiral, avoid ruble depreciation, and let the financial system weather the storm with minimum losses.
evidence.title: Elvira Nabiullina’s speech at joint meeting of State Duma dedicated committees on Bank of Russia’s 2022 Annual Report
evidence.excerpt: Nabiullina said the urgent measures taken after the early-2022 sanctions shock helped prevent an inflationary spiral, avoid ruble depreciation, and let the financial system weather the storm with minimum losses.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary official retrospective from the central bank head; strong for what the institution claims it achieved, but self-interested.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective on 2022 target-period policy and outcomes.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect but relevant: it describes the regime's crisis-management apparatus under Putin, though the institution itself executed the measures.
contrary_evidence: Self-reporting can overstate success.
It does not separate the effect of sanctions-driven import collapse from policy skill.

evidence.claim: Russia said it would temporarily stop foreign investors from selling Russian assets and would use its sovereign wealth fund to buy shares in Russian companies, framing the move as a response to sanctions.
evidence.title: Russia to temporarily ban foreigners from selling assets
evidence.excerpt: Russia said it would temporarily stop foreign investors from selling Russian assets and would use its sovereign wealth fund to buy shares in Russian companies, framing the move as a response to sanctions.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting on a government decree and a prime-minister statement; contemporaneous and specific, though mediated.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partial-to-strong: the restriction was a state response under Putin's government, though the direct announcement came via the prime minister.
contrary_evidence: Officials presented it as protecting jobs and making investors think carefully.
It may also be read as defensive crisis management rather than pure expropriation.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that United Russia said a government commission approved the first step toward nationalizing assets of foreign firms that leave, including a bill allowing firms more than 25% foreign-owned from unfriendly states to be put into external administration.
evidence.title: Russia moves towards nationalising assets of firms that leave - ruling party
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that United Russia said a government commission approved the first step toward nationalizing assets of foreign firms that leave, including a bill allowing firms more than 25% foreign-owned from unfriendly states to be put into external administration.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters contemporaneous report with clear legal-policy detail; the key claim is via ruling-party and commission statements.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year 2022, during the sanctions-driven corporate exodus.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong regime attribution: this was a Putin-era state response, even if the report cites the ruling party and commission rather than Putin personally.
contrary_evidence: The government framed it as preventing bankruptcy and saving jobs.
It does not by itself prove Putin personally ordered every asset case.

evidence.claim: Putin said he had signed a decree requiring foreign buyers to pay in roubles for Russian gas from April 1 or have contracts halted, explicitly tying the move to sovereignty and retaliation against sanctions.
evidence.title: Putin says Russia will enforce rouble payments for gas from Friday
evidence.excerpt: Putin said he had signed a decree requiring foreign buyers to pay in roubles for Russian gas from April 1 or have contracts halted, explicitly tying the move to sovereignty and retaliation against sanctions.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting of Putin's own televised decree and remarks; direct attribution and clear policy content.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year 2022, shortly after the invasion and sanctions.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct: this is a Putin decree and public threat to contracts and supply terms.
contrary_evidence: Putin claimed the move would strengthen sovereignty and preserve obligations.
The rouble strengthened partly because of this coercive demand, but the move also heightened energy-market instability.

evidence.claim: Russia's defence spending rose nearly 40% in the first four months of 2022, and the finance ministry said the budget was shifting from an expected surplus to at least a 1.6 trillion-ruble deficit because of sanctions and support payouts.
evidence.title: With troops in Ukraine, Russia's defence spending leaps 40%
evidence.excerpt: Russia's defence spending rose nearly 40% in the first four months of 2022, and the finance ministry said the budget was shifting from an expected surplus to at least a 1.6 trillion-ruble deficit because of sanctions and support payouts.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters report based on preliminary finance-ministry data; strong for budget direction, not for ultimate long-run effects.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year 2022, after the invasion and during wartime budget reallocation.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong: the spending surge and deficit shift were consequences of Putin's war choice and his government's fiscal priorities.
contrary_evidence: Some defense spending was a wartime necessity from the regime's own perspective.
A higher defense budget can be defended as security rather than prosperity policy, but it still crowds out civilian welfare.

evidence.claim: Reuters' budget analysis said Russia planned to spend nearly a third of the next year's budget on defence and domestic security while cutting funding for schools, hospitals, roads, national economy items, health, education, infrastructure, and R&D.
evidence.title: Analysis: Surge in Russia's defence and security spending means cuts for schools and hospitals in 2023
evidence.excerpt: Reuters' budget analysis said Russia planned to spend nearly a third of the next year's budget on defence and domestic security while cutting funding for schools, hospitals, roads, national economy items, health, education, infrastructure, and R&D.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters analysis based on budget documents and independent expert commentary; strong on spending priorities, though forward-looking.
evidence.period_fit: Late 2022 target-period decision shaping the 2023 budget trajectory.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong: the budget priorities reflect Putin's war-state priorities and his government's fiscal choices.
contrary_evidence: The article notes social spending still rose somewhat in nominal terms.
Officials could argue wartime priorities and patriotic training were strategic, but they still reduced civilian productivity spending.

evidence.claim: Russia recorded a budget deficit of 2.3% of GDP in 2022, reversing an earlier target surplus of 1% of GDP; the finance minister said the war burdened state finances and Putin had predicted a surplus only months earlier.
evidence.title: Russia says budget deficit hit 2.3% of GDP in 2022
evidence.excerpt: Russia recorded a budget deficit of 2.3% of GDP in 2022, reversing an earlier target surplus of 1% of GDP; the finance minister said the war burdened state finances and Putin had predicted a surplus only months earlier.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters report based on finance-ministry remarks and the minister's own figures; strong for the fiscal result.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective on the 2022 target-year fiscal outcome.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong: the deficit reflects the fiscal consequences of Putin's war and budget priorities, even if formal reporting came from the finance minister.
contrary_evidence: Some deficit pressure came from external sanctions and price-cap policy.
Russia still had room to borrow and draw on reserves, which softened the immediate fiscal collapse.

evidence.claim: Russia's annual inflation rate came in at 11.9% for 2022, according to Economy Minister Maxim Reshetnikov, after sharp price rises that followed sanctions imposed over the invasion of Ukraine.
evidence.title: Russian monthly inflation was 0.78% in December - Rosstat
evidence.excerpt: Russia's annual inflation rate came in at 11.9% for 2022, according to Economy Minister Maxim Reshetnikov, after sharp price rises that followed sanctions imposed over the invasion of Ukraine.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters report quoting the economy minister and Rosstat-reported price data; strong for the annual figure.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective on the 2022 target-year inflation outcome.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong on outcome, indirect on causation: the figure reflects the sanctions/invasion shock created by Putin's decision to invade.
contrary_evidence: Inflation later eased from the spring surge.
Price controls and capital controls also helped contain the peak, so the annual number is not pure policy failure alone.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that Russian consumer demand contracted at its fastest pace in seven years in 2022 and real disposable incomes fell 1%, with GDP down around 2.5% as sanctions and the war hit households.
evidence.title: Russia's 2022 economic fall seen in lower incomes, slumping consumer demand
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that Russian consumer demand contracted at its fastest pace in seven years in 2022 and real disposable incomes fell 1%, with GDP down around 2.5% as sanctions and the war hit households.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters cites official data and links it to the sanctions/war context; strong for household outcome, though causal attribution is partly contextual.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective on the 2022 target-year household outcome.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong on outcome and medium on causation: the drop is tied to Putin's war choice and sanctions response, though some effects were cushioned by state support and export revenues.
contrary_evidence: Wages rose slightly in late 2022, so the household picture was mixed.
Some consumer-demand weakness could reflect wartime mobilization rather than only economic policy.

evidence.claim: Rosstat said Russia's economy contracted by 1.2% in 2022, and Reuters noted that Western sanctions followed Putin's decision to send troops into Ukraine.
evidence.title: Russian economy shrank by 1.2% in 2022, less than previously thought - stats service
evidence.excerpt: Rosstat said Russia's economy contracted by 1.2% in 2022, and Reuters noted that Western sanctions followed Putin's decision to send troops into Ukraine.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters report of the official statistics-service revision; strong for the final 2022 GDP figure.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective on the 2022 target-year GDP outcome.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong on overall outcome attribution: the contraction is explicitly linked to Putin's invasion decision, though later revisions and wartime spending complicate exact magnitude.
contrary_evidence: The final contraction was smaller than earlier estimates, so the immediate collapse was limited.
War spending later supported measured growth, but that does not change the 2022 loss in civilian prosperity.

decisive_positive_evidence.explanation: The central bank still showed some capacity to stabilize markets under stress.
Rate cuts later in 2022 reflected partial stabilization after the shock.
The central bank claimed its emergency measures prevented a worse spiral.

decisive_negative_evidence.explanation: The gas rouble-payment decree intensified coercive economic pressure and sanctions conflict.
Defense spending surged and the budget shifted sharply into deficit.
The economy contracted in 2022 because of the invasion and sanctions shock.

judge.inherited_baseline_and_constraints: Russia entered 2022 with a relatively strong pre-war macro position, but Putin's invasion created the central constraint: sanctions, war spending, and coercive economic policy rapidly replaced ordinary prosperity management.
judge.ruler_attribution: Attribution is extremely strong for the main negatives because they follow directly from Putin's war and coercive choices; the positives are mostly crisis containment by technocratic institutions he retained.

contrary_evidence.explanation: There was some macro stabilization and institutional resilience, so the score is not a flat zero.
The central bank says emergency measures prevented an even worse financial collapse.

judge.source_mix: Reuters-based reporting, Bank of Russia releases, and official fiscal data; no structured local priors were collected in this experiment.
judge.structured_prior_summary: Structured local priors were unavailable across all lenses; the judgment relies on the dossier evidence and source-confidence metadata only.
judge.chapter_rationale: Putin scores 1.5 because the 2022 record is defined by a war of choice that destroyed broad prosperity, cut household demand and incomes, and forced the economy into coercive, militarized adjustment. The only meaningful positives are technocratic crisis containment and partial stabilization, but those do not outweigh the direct negative effects of invasion, sanctions, inflation, and war spending. This is far below a normal mixed record: it is a severe prosperity destruction case, just short of the realized-catastrophe floor reserved for the most extreme outcomes.
judge.lower_anchor_rejected: A score of 1 would reserve the absolute floor for a realized nuclear or equivalent catastrophe; this file, while devastating, is an economic-war destruction case rather than that floor.
judge.higher_anchor_rejected: A score near 3 would ignore the direct contraction, inflation, household-income loss, and militarized fiscal shift documented here.

chapter_specific.value: The trajectory collapsed from pre-war stability into war economy, contraction, and coercive adaptation.
Sanctions mattered, but the central external condition was Putin's own invasion decision, which triggered the collapse.
Household demand and real incomes fell, and the prosperity burden was broad rather than confined to elites.

judge.reader_abstract:
Overall, Vladimir Putin's record on economic well-being in 2022 was assessed as poor, resulting in a score of 1.5 out of 10.

Evidence supporting a more favorable assessment includes the following: Reuters reported that Elvira Nabiullina resisted calls from powerful industrialists and the Economy Ministry for interest-rate cuts, and a cited economist said she must have had Putin's support to do this; and Rate cuts later in 2022 reflected partial stabilization after the shock.

Evidence weighing against a stronger assessment includes the following: Putin said he had signed a decree requiring foreign buyers to pay in roubles for Russian gas from April 1 or have contracts halted, explicitly tying the move to sovereignty and retaliation against sanctions; and Russia's defence spending rose nearly 40% in the first four months of 2022, and the finance ministry said the budget was shifting from an expected surplus to at least a 1.6 trillion-ruble deficit because of sanctions and support payouts.

Responsibility and evidentiary limits matter here: Attribution is extremely strong for the main negatives because they follow directly from Putin's war and coercive choices; the positives are mostly crisis containment by technocratic institutions he retained.

Taken together, I did not go higher because a score near 3 would ignore the direct contraction, inflation, household-income loss, and militarized fiscal shift documented here. I did not go lower because a score of 1 would reserve the absolute floor for a realized nuclear or equivalent catastrophe; this file, while devastating, is an economic-war destruction case rather than that floor.

evidence.claim: Putin approved instructions requiring the government to create a special procedure to assess families whose members lost jobs after March 1, 2022, expand access to social support for families with children whose income fell, add support for the unemployed, index pensions and social benefits, raise the minimum wage and subsistence minimum, and allocate federal funds for regional support and infrastructure.
evidence.title: Instructions following a meeting on socioeconomic support for regions
evidence.excerpt: Putin approved instructions requiring the government to create a special procedure to assess families whose members lost jobs after March 1, 2022, expand access to social support for families with children whose income fell, add support for the unemployed, index pensions and social benefits, raise the minimum wage and subsistence minimum, and allocate federal funds for regional support and infrastructure.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct presidential instructions on a dated 2022 policy package; the page states the specific actions and implementation deadlines.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and tied to Putin's formal authority.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct: Putin approved the instructions and tasked the government; implementation depended on ministries and regional authorities.
contrary_evidence: The order is reactive crisis management during war and sanctions, not proof of durable welfare improvement.
Benefits were mediated by government and regional implementation.

evidence.claim: Rosstat said 2022 poverty was 9.8% (14.3 million people), down from 11.0% in 2021, and that targeted state support in 2022 reduced income differentiation; the correction was based on household survey and administrative data.
evidence.title: Росстат уточнил данные о численности населения с доходами ниже границы бедности в 2022 году
evidence.excerpt: Rosstat said 2022 poverty was 9.8% (14.3 million people), down from 11.0% in 2021, and that targeted state support in 2022 reduced income differentiation; the correction was based on household survey and administrative data.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official statistical revision with named methodology and sample size, but still a state source and not independent of policy claims.
evidence.period_fit: Covers the target year 2022, though published in 2023 after revision.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partial: the statistic reflects state social support under Putin, but also wages, prices, and measurement revisions.
contrary_evidence: Official framing may over-credit policy and understate wartime inflation or regional disparities.
Poverty remained substantial despite the decline.

evidence.claim: Rosstat said the 8-17 child cash benefit introduced on April 1, 2022 covered 3.7 million families and more than 5.5 million children during 2022, while social payments and targeted social programs were a main driver of lower poverty.
evidence.title: Росстат представляет информацию о границе бедности в IV квартале 2022 года
evidence.excerpt: Rosstat said the 8-17 child cash benefit introduced on April 1, 2022 covered 3.7 million families and more than 5.5 million children during 2022, while social payments and targeted social programs were a main driver of lower poverty.
evidence.source_locator: poverty section / social support bullet points
evidence.source_confidence_reason: The page gives explicit beneficiary counts and links them to social payments, but it is an official statistical communication and should be corroborated.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers 2022 implementation and beneficiary reach.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partial to direct: the benefit expansion was a 2022 state policy under Putin, but delivery and take-up depend on administrative execution.
contrary_evidence: Coverage counts do not show adequacy, equality, or who was excluded.
The same source still shows millions below the poverty line.

evidence.claim: UNICEF's Russia SDG dashboard shows that 100% of children were covered by social protection floors/systems in 2020, while 12% of children were below the national poverty line in 2020 and 0% were in extreme poverty in 2022.
evidence.title: Child-Related SDG Progress Assessment for Russian Federation
evidence.excerpt: UNICEF's Russia SDG dashboard shows that 100% of children were covered by social protection floors/systems in 2020, while 12% of children were below the national poverty line in 2020 and 0% were in extreme poverty in 2022.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: UNICEF compiles internationally comparable indicator data, but this page is a dashboard with lagged indicator years and not ruler-specific causal attribution.
evidence.period_fit: Lagged indicators around the target year; useful as baseline/context rather than direct 2022 policy proof.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly inherited/system-level context; it does not isolate Putin's 2022 marginal contribution.
contrary_evidence: The social protection coverage indicator is from 2020 rather than 2022.
Dashboard indicators do not prove service quality or inclusion for all groups.

evidence.claim: UNICEF's dashboard reports that Russian Federation had 97% DTP3 coverage in 2022, 100% skilled birth attendance in 2020, and an under-five mortality rate of 5 per 1,000 live births in 2021.
evidence.title: Child-Related SDG Progress Assessment for Russian Federation
evidence.excerpt: UNICEF's dashboard reports that Russian Federation had 97% DTP3 coverage in 2022, 100% skilled birth attendance in 2020, and an under-five mortality rate of 5 per 1,000 live births in 2021.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Global indicator dashboard with lagged years; useful for baseline but not direct ruler attribution.
evidence.period_fit: Near-target-year health outcome indicators, but not a 2022 policy act.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly inherited/system-level context; limited evidence of marginal improvement attributable to Putin in 2022.
contrary_evidence: Health outcomes lag policy and may reflect earlier investments rather than 2022 actions.
Indicator coverage does not show regional or class disparities.

evidence.claim: WHO says Russia has universal health coverage with free care in state and municipal facilities, but quality and availability vary widely by region; the basic package is set federally while territorial packages can differ.
evidence.title: Russian Federation health system information
evidence.publisher: WHO European Observatory on Health Systems and Policies
evidence.excerpt: WHO says Russia has universal health coverage with free care in state and municipal facilities, but quality and availability vary widely by region; the basic package is set federally while territorial packages can differ.
evidence.source_locator: country profile / health system overview lines 150-151
evidence.source_confidence_reason: WHO/Observatory synthesis is authoritative on system design, though it describes structure rather than 2022 performance.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly inherited institutional context; it does not by itself show Putin strengthened or weakened service delivery in 2022.
contrary_evidence: Universal coverage does not guarantee equal quality or access.
Regional variation limits direct inference about nationwide welfare gains.

evidence.claim: WHO's country data says life expectancy at birth in Russia improved by 4.86 years from 65.2 in 2000 to 70.0 in 2021, and healthy life expectancy improved by 4.23 years over the same period.
evidence.title: Russian Federation
evidence.excerpt: WHO's country data says life expectancy at birth in Russia improved by 4.86 years from 65.2 in 2000 to 70.0 in 2021, and healthy life expectancy improved by 4.23 years over the same period.
evidence.source_locator: life expectancy / healthy life expectancy country overview
evidence.source_confidence_reason: WHO country data are a standard source for health outcomes, but the figures are lagged and not a 2022 policy attribution on their own.
evidence.period_fit: Latest available health trajectory close to 2022; not direct 2022 policymaking evidence.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Inherited long-run trajectory more than Putin-specific 2022 action; use cautiously as baseline and trend context.
contrary_evidence: The page does not isolate 2022 or Putin's specific contribution.
Health gains may reflect earlier decades and non-Putin factors.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that Russian consumer demand contracted at its fastest pace in seven years in 2022, real disposable incomes fell 1%, retail sales dropped 6.7%, and unemployment stayed low at 3.7%, while top officials linked the labor-market strain to mobilization and sanctions.
evidence.title: Russia's 2022 economic fall seen in lower incomes, slumping consumer demand
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that Russian consumer demand contracted at its fastest pace in seven years in 2022, real disposable incomes fell 1%, retail sales dropped 6.7%, and unemployment stayed low at 3.7%, while top officials linked the labor-market strain to mobilization and sanctions.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters is a strong wire-service source, and the passage cites Rosstat data with concrete 2022 household outcomes.
evidence.period_fit: Directly about 2022 household outcomes, published early 2023.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong on negative attribution to Putin's invasion and mobilization decisions; some components also reflect sanctions and preexisting labor-market conditions.
contrary_evidence: Low unemployment is a partial positive counterpoint.
The article notes the economy withstood sanctions better than first expected.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that Russia's 2022 budget deficit reached 2.3% of GDP, below a prewar surplus target, because of the Ukraine war's burden on state finances and a shift toward security and defence spending.
evidence.title: Russia says budget deficit hit 2.3% of GDP in 2022
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that Russia's 2022 budget deficit reached 2.3% of GDP, below a prewar surplus target, because of the Ukraine war's burden on state finances and a shift toward security and defence spending.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters quotes the finance minister and states the budget consequence clearly.
evidence.period_fit: Directly about 2022 fiscal outcomes and wartime spending choices.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong: the deficit and reallocation are consequences of Putin's war and budget priorities, though the precise fiscal line is implemented by the finance ministry.
contrary_evidence: A deficit is not by itself proof of social welfare failure; some spending was countercyclical support.
Oil revenues and domestic borrowing softened the immediate shock.

evidence.claim: The World Bank said Russian poverty could rise to 14.1% in 2020 without fully compensatory measures, and that existing social protection programs announced in January, March, and April 2020 could partly compensate for crisis impacts on families with children, the unemployed, and SMEs.
evidence.title: COVID-19 (Coronavirus) Policy Response to Protecting the Poorest and Most Vulnerable in Russia
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank said Russian poverty could rise to 14.1% in 2020 without fully compensatory measures, and that existing social protection programs announced in January, March, and April 2020 could partly compensate for crisis impacts on families with children, the unemployed, and SMEs.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: World Bank analysis is methodologically stronger than political advocacy, but it is a forecast and predates the target year.
evidence.period_fit: Pre-2022 baseline context on crisis response capacity and welfare architecture.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly baseline and institutional context; it shows preexisting social protection channels rather than Putin-specific 2022 improvement.
contrary_evidence: It is a 2020 forecast, not a 2022 outcome.
The measures are described as partial compensation rather than a solution.

evidence.excerpt: The World Bank said schoolchildren in Russia were at risk of learning losses of up to six months, that poor and under-represented students were more likely to suffer dropout or lower qualifications, and that Russia moved to distance-learning measures and digital platforms.
evidence.source_locator: challenges / what Russia has done to confront these challenges

contrary_evidence: It is about COVID-era disruption, not 2022 social policy.
The brief is about risks and mitigation, not demonstrated outcome improvement.

decisive_positive_evidence.explanation: Putin ordered targeted support for families, pension indexation, unemployment support, and regional funds.
Rosstat later reported poverty down and said targeted support helped reduce income differentiation.
Child cash benefits covered millions of families and children.

decisive_negative_evidence.explanation: Consumer demand contracted, disposable incomes fell, and retail sales dropped in 2022.
The budget moved to a wartime deficit and heavier security spending, crowding out ordinary welfare priorities.
The system-level health profile shows regional inequality and uneven access, limiting welfare credit.

judge.inherited_baseline_and_constraints: Russia entered 2022 with a functioning welfare state but the year was transformed by war, mobilization, sanctions, and fiscal reorientation. That combination means social support exists, but the chapter must heavily discount it because the ruler's own war choices worsened ordinary life chances.
judge.ruler_attribution: The harm is strongly attributable to Putin through war and budget priorities, while the positive social supports are government-mediated and only partially offset the damage. Direct ruler causation is much clearer on the negative side than the positive side.

contrary_evidence.explanation: Household incomes and consumer demand fell sharply, which substantially outweighs the targeted supports.
Wartime fiscal deterioration and higher security spending show the welfare environment was weakened overall.

judge.source_mix: Official Russian statistics and presidential instructions combined with Reuters and WHO/UNICEF/World Bank context. The dossier is strong on reactive support but even stronger on war-linked welfare damage.
judge.structured_prior_summary: Structured local priors were not collected in this experiment, so the judgment relies on the embedded dossier evidence, the reviewer exclusions already present there, and cross-case calibration within the batch.
judge.chapter_rationale: Putin gets a low score because 2022 combines some real cash support and poverty mitigation with a much more important pattern of war-driven deterioration in living standards. The welfare measures are not nothing, but they are reactive and partially compensatory, while incomes, consumer demand, and fiscal balance all worsened under the broader wartime course. That places the dossier in the lower band, though not at the absolute floor because the state still maintained targeted support channels.
judge.lower_anchor_rejected: A lower score would ignore the fact that the regime still delivered meaningful cash support and child benefits to large populations.
judge.higher_anchor_rejected: A higher score would require evidence that the welfare state improved ordinary life chances despite the war, which the dossier does not show.

chapter_specific.value: cash transfers, pensions, child benefits, regional support
families with children, the unemployed, and low-income households are targeted, but war harms dominate
war, sanctions, and mobilization reshape the welfare record
reactive support exists, but overall life chances deteriorate

judge.reader_abstract:
Overall, Vladimir Putin's record on social well-being in 2022 was assessed as poor, resulting in a score of 3 out of 10.

Evidence supporting a more favorable assessment includes the following: Putin approved instructions requiring the government to create a special procedure to assess families whose members lost jobs after March 1, 2022, expand access to social support for families with children whose income fell, add support for the unemployed, index pensions and social benefits, raise the minimum wage and subsistence minimum, and allocate federal funds for regional support and infrastructure; and Rosstat said 2022 poverty was 9.8% (14.3 million people), down from 11.0% in 2021, and that targeted state support in 2022 reduced income differentiation; the correction was based on household survey and administrative data.

Evidence weighing against a stronger assessment includes the following: Reuters reported that Russian consumer demand contracted at its fastest pace in seven years in 2022, real disposable incomes fell 1%, retail sales dropped 6.7%, and unemployment stayed low at 3.7%, while top officials linked the labor-market strain to mobilization and sanctions; and Reuters reported that Russia's 2022 budget deficit reached 2.3% of GDP, below a prewar surplus target, because of the Ukraine war's burden on state finances and a shift toward security and defence spending.

Responsibility and evidentiary limits matter here: The harm is strongly attributable to Putin through war and budget priorities, while the positive social supports are government-mediated and only partially offset the damage. Direct ruler causation is much clearer on the negative side than the positive side.

Taken together, I did not go higher because a higher score would require evidence that the welfare state improved ordinary life chances despite the war, which the dossier does not show. I did not go lower because a lower score would ignore the fact that the regime still delivered meaningful cash support and child benefits to large populations.

evidence.claim: Putin proposed nominating Elvira Nabiullina for a third term in a bid to ensure macroeconomic stability, and Reuters noted she was a committed inflation fighter resisting pressure for rate cuts.
evidence.title: Putin tips central bank chief Nabiullina for third term to ensure economic stability
evidence.excerpt: Putin proposed nominating Elvira Nabiullina for a third term in a bid to ensure macroeconomic stability, and Reuters noted she was a committed inflation fighter resisting pressure for rate cuts.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters contemporaneous report based on a Kremlin spokesman and clear attribution of the nomination proposal.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year 2022; direct personnel decision during the sanctions shock.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct on the nomination proposal; partially indirect on monetary-policy empowerment because the central bank sets rates independently, but Putin's retention choice mattered.
contrary_evidence: The Bank of Russia still acted as an institution with some independence.
This says little about whether the broader economic agenda favored broad-based prosperity.

evidence.claim: Putin, his spokesman, and other Russian officials repeatedly denied that Russia planned to invade Ukraine; that denial was proved false when Russia launched a full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.
evidence.title: Russian Rhetoric Ahead of Attack Against Ukraine: Deny, Deflect, Mislead
evidence.excerpt: Putin, his spokesman, and other Russian officials repeatedly denied that Russia planned to invade Ukraine; that denial was proved false when Russia launched a full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: The article collates contemporaneous denials and directly checks them against the invasion outcome in the same week.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers February 2022 statements and the target-year invasion.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Putin and his immediate public messaging, though the article groups him with other officials rather than isolating a single quote.
contrary_evidence: The piece does not provide a sworn admission by Putin; it shows the denial pattern and then the falsifying event.

evidence.claim: OFAC said Putin uses complex support networks to hide and move money and anonymously use luxury assets; it identified Graceful and Olympia as blocked property in which Putin has an interest and said Sergei Roldugin is a custodian of Putin’s offshore wealth.
evidence.title: U.S. Treasury Severs More Networks Providing Support for Putin and Russia’s Elites
evidence.excerpt: OFAC said Putin uses complex support networks to hide and move money and anonymously use luxury assets; it identified Graceful and Olympia as blocked property in which Putin has an interest and said Sergei Roldugin is a custodian of Putin’s offshore wealth.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: This is an official sanctions finding with named assets, named intermediaries, and explicit attribution language.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong official attribution, though the underlying ownership chain is intentionally opaque and the Kremlin denied the links.
contrary_evidence: The Kremlin denied affiliation with the assets; the precise beneficial-ownership chain remains partly hidden.

evidence.claim: HRW said Navalny’s March 22, 2022 conviction on new charges was a mockery of justice intended to silence him; the authorities also accused him of embezzling donations for personal gain.
evidence.title: Russia: Kremlin Targets Critics Amid Ukraine War
evidence.excerpt: HRW said Navalny’s March 22, 2022 conviction on new charges was a mockery of justice intended to silence him; the authorities also accused him of embezzling donations for personal gain.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous rights-monitoring report with explicit description of the prosecution’s political function and the contested embezzlement allegations.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strongly attributable to Putin’s government because the prosecution and sentence were carried out by state institutions under his rule, targeting his leading anti-corruption critic.
contrary_evidence: The embezzlement allegation is reported as the authorities’ claim and remains contested in the article.

evidence.claim: Navalny launched an international anti-corruption organization after his Russian Anti-Corruption Foundation was outlawed as extremist, and Reuters said his foundation had catalogued the wealth of senior Russian officials.
evidence.title: Russia's Navalny launches international anti-corruption fund
evidence.excerpt: Navalny launched an international anti-corruption organization after his Russian Anti-Corruption Foundation was outlawed as extremist, and Reuters said his foundation had catalogued the wealth of senior Russian officials.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters-syndicated reporting with a clear 2022 dateline; the article directly connects the anti-corruption crackdown to the outlawing of the foundation.
evidence.period_fit: Within 2022 and directly relevant to the treatment of anti-corruption scrutiny.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strongly attributable to the Putin system because the article says the court ruling outlawing ACF empowered authorities to jail activists and freeze accounts.
contrary_evidence: This is a report about Navalny’s response rather than a direct Putin quote or order.

evidence.claim: Authorities opened a new criminal case against Navalny for promoting terrorism and extremism, potentially more than doubling his sentence; Navalny said the existing convictions were trumped-up charges intended to silence him.
evidence.title: Russia's Navalny says he faces new criminal case for 'promoting terrorism'
evidence.excerpt: Authorities opened a new criminal case against Navalny for promoting terrorism and extremism, potentially more than doubling his sentence; Navalny said the existing convictions were trumped-up charges intended to silence him.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters report syndicated by Euronews with a 2022 dateline; the article gives the prosecution and Navalny’s response in the same piece.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year 2022, with the new case announced in October.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strongly attributable to Putin’s governing apparatus, though the article does not include an immediate official confirmation from investigators.
contrary_evidence: The article says there was no immediate official confirmation from the Investigative Committee.

decisive_positive_evidence.explanation: The denials of invasion plans were directly falsified by the February 24 invasion, making this a clear honesty failure.
The Treasury sanctions finding on hidden luxury assets and support networks is strong evidence of concealment and personal opacity.
The Navalny prosecution as a 'mockery of justice' reflects state power being used to suppress a critic who documented official corruption.
The new criminal case against Navalny reinforces the pattern of retaliatory accountability suppression under Putin's system.

decisive_negative_evidence.explanation: Retaining Nabiullina as central bank chief is a real technocratic counterexample, but it does not outweigh the broader concealment and deception record.
The anti-corruption-organization context shows the regime was responding to scrutiny, even if repressively.

judge.inherited_baseline_and_constraints: No structured local priors were collected. Russia's closed information environment is not used as a substitute for proof; the score is driven by the direct invasion denial, sanctions findings, and repression of critics.
judge.ruler_attribution: Direct and strong on concealment, misleading public messaging, and state-backed retaliation. Personal-benefit proof is strongest where sanctions identify hidden luxury assets and support networks, while the state uses power to neutralize scrutiny.

contrary_evidence.explanation: One technocratic retention decision keeps the file from becoming pure caricature.
The broader anti-corruption context exists, but it is used repressively rather than transparently.

judge.source_mix: Reuters, U.S. Treasury sanctions material, fact-checking, and human-rights reporting. Strongest on direct falsity, hidden assets, and repression; weaker only where ownership chains remain intentionally opaque.
judge.structured_prior_summary: Local priors unavailable in this experiment; judgment uses the embedded dossier only.
judge.chapter_rationale: Putin is one of the lowest scores because the dossier shows a direct public denial that was disproved by the invasion, an official sanctions finding about hidden wealth and support networks, and repeated use of state power against Navalny and anti-corruption scrutiny. That is a classic pattern of concealment and impunity. The presence of one technocratic economic appointment keeps the case from becoming a total one-note caricature, but not by much. The record is strong enough to justify a near-floor score without invoking the broader war or repression context as a substitute for ruler-specific integrity evidence.
judge.lower_anchor_rejected: A score of 1 would require either a still more extreme personal extraction record or a realized catastrophic event in this chapter, which is not what 7B measures. This file is extremely bad, but the evidence is still about honesty and concealment rather than a full kleptocratic canon with direct trial findings on everything.
judge.higher_anchor_rejected: A score of 3 or above would understate the centrality of the false invasion denial, sanctions findings on hidden assets, and retaliatory prosecutions. The dishonesty pattern is too strong.
judge.reader_abstract:
Overall, Vladimir Putin's record on integrity in 2022 was assessed as poor, resulting in a score of 2 out of 10.

Evidence supporting a more favorable assessment includes the following: Putin, his spokesman, and other Russian officials repeatedly denied that Russia planned to invade Ukraine; that denial was proved false when Russia launched a full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022; and OFAC said Putin uses complex support networks to hide and move money and anonymously use luxury assets; it identified Graceful and Olympia as blocked property in which Putin has an interest and said Sergei Roldugin is a custodian of Putin’s offshore wealth.

Evidence weighing against a stronger assessment includes the following: Putin proposed nominating Elvira Nabiullina for a third term in a bid to ensure macroeconomic stability, and Reuters noted she was a committed inflation fighter resisting pressure for rate cuts; and Navalny launched an international anti-corruption organization after his Russian Anti-Corruption Foundation was outlawed as extremist, and Reuters said his foundation had catalogued the wealth of senior Russian officials.

Responsibility and evidentiary limits matter here: Direct and strong on concealment, misleading public messaging, and state-backed retaliation. Personal-benefit proof is strongest where sanctions identify hidden luxury assets and support networks, while the state uses power to neutralize scrutiny.

Taken together, I did not go higher because a score of 3 or above would understate the centrality of the false invasion denial, sanctions findings on hidden assets, and retaliatory prosecutions. The dishonesty pattern is too strong. I did not go lower because a score of 1 would require either a still more extreme personal extraction record or a realized catastrophic event in this chapter, which is not what 7B measures. This file is extremely bad, but the evidence is still about honesty and concealment rather than a full kleptocratic canon with direct trial findings on everything.

evidence.claim: Putin authorized the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and said the goal was to demilitarise and 'denazify' Ukraine.

evidence.excerpt: Putin authorized the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and said the goal was to demilitarise and 'denazify' Ukraine.

evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct personal attribution to Putin
contrary_evidence: The Kremlin framed the operation as defensive.
The report shows the operational choice was still an invasion.

evidence.claim: Putin announced partial mobilization, tied the war to defense of territorial integrity, and said Russia would use all available means, adding that the warning was not bluff.
evidence.title: Address by the President of the Russian Federation
evidence.excerpt: Putin announced partial mobilization, tied the war to defense of territorial integrity, and said Russia would use all available means, adding that the warning was not bluff.
evidence.source_locator: speech transcript paragraphs containing the territorial-integrity and 'not bluff' language
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official Kremlin transcript of a live presidential address with direct attribution.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct personal attribution to Putin
contrary_evidence: The Kremlin said the warning was defensive.
The speech escalated the war and widened coercive pressure.

evidence.claim: Meduza reported that Russia's State Duma ratified treaties on the 'admission' of the DNR, LNR, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson, formalizing the annexation package Putin had signed.
evidence.title: Госдума единогласно одобрила аннексию оккупированных украинских территорий
evidence.excerpt: Meduza reported that Russia's State Duma ratified treaties on the 'admission' of the DNR, LNR, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson, formalizing the annexation package Putin had signed.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent Russian-language reporting on the ratification of Putin's annexation treaties.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly tied to Putin's treaty-signing and Russia's state apparatus
contrary_evidence: The article itself notes these were occupied Ukrainian territories.
The ratification did not alter international law's rejection of the annexation.

evidence.claim: Russia's annual inflation rate came in at 11.9% for 2022, according to Economy Minister Maxim Reshetnikov, after sharp price rises that followed sanctions imposed over the invasion of Ukraine.
evidence.title: Russian monthly inflation was 0.78% in December - Rosstat
evidence.excerpt: Russia's annual inflation rate came in at 11.9% for 2022, according to Economy Minister Maxim Reshetnikov, after sharp price rises that followed sanctions imposed over the invasion of Ukraine.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters report quoting the economy minister and Rosstat-reported price data; strong for the annual figure.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective on the 2022 target-year inflation outcome.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong on outcome, indirect on causation: the figure reflects the sanctions/invasion shock created by Putin's decision to invade.
contrary_evidence: Inflation later eased from the spring surge.
Price controls and capital controls also helped contain the peak, so the annual number is not pure policy failure alone.

evidence.claim: Rosstat said Russia's economy contracted by 1.2% in 2022, and Reuters noted that Western sanctions followed Putin's decision to send troops into Ukraine.
evidence.title: Russian economy shrank by 1.2% in 2022, less than previously thought - stats service
evidence.excerpt: Rosstat said Russia's economy contracted by 1.2% in 2022, and Reuters noted that Western sanctions followed Putin's decision to send troops into Ukraine.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters report of the official statistics-service revision; strong for the final 2022 GDP figure.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective on the 2022 target-year GDP outcome.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong on overall outcome attribution: the contraction is explicitly linked to Putin's invasion decision, though later revisions and wartime spending complicate exact magnitude.
contrary_evidence: The final contraction was smaller than earlier estimates, so the immediate collapse was limited.
War spending later supported measured growth, but that does not change the 2022 loss in civilian prosperity.

evidence.claim: Putin said the operation's goal was to protect people in Donbas and to demilitarise and denazify Ukraine, making the war's core aim explicit.
evidence.title: Russia's Putin authorises 'special military operation' against Ukraine
evidence.excerpt: Putin said the operation's goal was to protect people in Donbas and to demilitarise and denazify Ukraine, making the war's core aim explicit.
evidence.source_locator: Reuters lead paragraph / quoted address in search result snippet
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous Reuters reporting on Putin's own televised announcement; direct quote and immediate publication date match the target period.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within the 2022 target period and program origin point.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct and strong; this is Putin's own public statement, though self-justifying and contested by Ukraine and Western governments.
contrary_evidence: Ukraine and Western officials characterized the invasion as an imperialist war, not a protective operation.

evidence.claim: Moscow signalled it was scaling back its ambitions in Ukraine to focus on Donbass, saying the first phase was mostly complete and that the main goal was the 'liberation of Donbass'.
evidence.title: Russia reframes war goals as Ukrainians advance near Kyiv
evidence.excerpt: Moscow signalled it was scaling back its ambitions in Ukraine to focus on Donbass, saying the first phase was mostly complete and that the main goal was the 'liberation of Donbass'.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting with a precise date and a concrete statement by the Russian defence ministry during the 2022 campaign.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and squarely about execution of the war program.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong but indirect; the statement came from the Russian defence ministry under Putin's rule and was used to justify a course correction after setbacks.
contrary_evidence: The same report says Russian troops had failed to capture any major city in the first month and were being pushed back near Kyiv.

evidence.claim: Russia said it would sharply reduce military activity around Kyiv and Chernihiv to increase mutual trust and create conditions for further negotiations.
evidence.title: Russia says it will sharply cut military activity near Kyiv, Chernihiv
evidence.excerpt: Russia said it would sharply reduce military activity around Kyiv and Chernihiv to increase mutual trust and create conditions for further negotiations.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters report on a specific operational pause announced after Istanbul talks; the claim is temporally and causally well anchored.
evidence.period_fit: Within the target year and directly about tactical adaptation in the war.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strongly attributable to Putin's war leadership, though the announcement was made by the Russian military delegation rather than Putin personally.
contrary_evidence: The reduction did not cover Russian offensives elsewhere and was widely read as a repositioning after setbacks.

evidence.claim: Putin approved instructions to expand support for families that lost income or jobs after March 1, 2022, increase pensions, social benefits, wages, minimum wage and subsistence minimum, fund regional budgets and infrastructure, and bring down poverty and income inequality.
evidence.title: Instructions following a meeting on socioeconomic support for regions
evidence.excerpt: Putin approved instructions to expand support for families that lost income or jobs after March 1, 2022, increase pensions, social benefits, wages, minimum wage and subsistence minimum, fund regional budgets and infrastructure, and bring down poverty and income inequality.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official presidential instructions with concrete deadlines, fiscal channels, and implementation tasks.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and tightly tied to wartime domestic management.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct; the instructions were approved by Putin and delegated to government bodies for implementation.
contrary_evidence: This is a directive package, not proof that all intended measures were fully delivered on time.

evidence.claim: Putin ordered Russia's first mobilisation since World War Two after a major battlefield reversal, with Shoigu saying 300,000 reservists would be drafted to support the war in Ukraine.
evidence.title: Russia calls up 300,000 reservists, says 6,000 soldiers killed in Ukraine
evidence.excerpt: Putin ordered Russia's first mobilisation since World War Two after a major battlefield reversal, with Shoigu saying 300,000 reservists would be drafted to support the war in Ukraine.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting on a major 2022 strategic decision and its immediate implementation parameters.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within the target year and a central adaptation point.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong; the mobilisation followed Putin's order and was part of the state response to battlefield reversals under his command.
contrary_evidence: The same story reports heavy casualties and frames the mobilisation as a response to setbacks rather than evidence of prior success.

evidence.claim: Russia exempted some bankers, IT workers and journalists from mobilisation in order to keep critical industries and the financial system functioning smoothly.
evidence.title: Russia excludes some IT professionals, bankers and journalists from mobilisation
evidence.excerpt: Russia exempted some bankers, IT workers and journalists from mobilisation in order to keep critical industries and the financial system functioning smoothly.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reports an explicit policy exception with stated operational rationale from the central bank and defence ministry.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within the target year and part of wartime implementation.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strongly attributable to Putin's governing network, though the measure is implemented by ministries and the central bank rather than Putin personally.
contrary_evidence: The exemptions also reveal that mobilisation was causing practical strain and required improvisation.

evidence.claim: Russia's Defence Ministry named Sergei Surovikin overall commander of forces fighting in Ukraine after a series of dramatic reverses, as part of an effort to centralise command and control.
evidence.title: Russia names air force general to lead its forces in Ukraine
evidence.excerpt: Russia's Defence Ministry named Sergei Surovikin overall commander of forces fighting in Ukraine after a series of dramatic reverses, as part of an effort to centralise command and control.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters coverage of a major command reshuffle with explicit mention of the operational rationale.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and clearly part of wartime adaptation.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong; the command change occurred under Putin's war leadership, though the ministerial chain executed it.
contrary_evidence: Command changes can indicate failure as well as adaptation; the appointment does not itself prove improved battlefield performance.

evidence.claim: Russia said it had completed its withdrawal from Kherson, a lightning-fast retreat of tens of thousands of troops that Reuters described as a major setback and the loss of the only regional capital Russia captured after the invasion.
evidence.title: Russia says it has completed retreat from Kherson
evidence.excerpt: Russia said it had completed its withdrawal from Kherson, a lightning-fast retreat of tens of thousands of troops that Reuters described as a major setback and the loss of the only regional capital Russia captured after the invasion.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters report with clear attribution and detailed battlefield consequences; the article provides a strong negative outcome marker for the war program.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and decisive for end-of-year war performance.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong; the withdrawal was ordered by Russia's defence ministry under Putin's overall war authority, though Surovikin and Shoigu handled the immediate decision.
contrary_evidence: Russian officials framed the move as an orderly transfer to defensive lines and said they were still committed to the operation's goals.

evidence.claim: Putin told defence-industry chiefs that the key task was to provide frontline units with weapons, equipment, ammunition and gear in the necessary quantities and shortest timeframes.
evidence.title: Putin tells Russian defence industry to up its game for Ukraine war
evidence.excerpt: Putin told defence-industry chiefs that the key task was to provide frontline units with weapons, equipment, ammunition and gear in the necessary quantities and shortest timeframes.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters published this as a concrete wartime directive from Putin to the industrial base.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and tied to execution of the war program.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct; this is Putin personally tasking the industrial base under wartime conditions.

decisive_positive_evidence.explanation: Putin directly launched the full-scale invasion, showing unambiguous command and mobilization.
The partial-mobilization announcement shows further state mobilization under his authority.
The mass call-up of reservists shows the regime could still mobilize coercive resources.
Direct instructions to the defense industry show active wartime management of the industrial base.

decisive_negative_evidence.explanation: The Kherson retreat is a major setback and strong evidence of strategic failure.
The economy contracted in 2022, directly tied to the invasion and sanctions shock he created.
Inflation remained high after the invasion, showing major collateral damage to domestic stability.

judge.inherited_baseline_and_constraints: Putin inherited a large coercive state and used it to launch war, annex territory, and mobilize society. But the 2022 record is dominated by strategic overreach and battlefield setbacks, so inherited state capacity cannot offset the visible program failure by year-end.
judge.ruler_attribution: Direct and strong across the central war decisions. Unlike many dossiers, attribution is not the problem; the problem is that the program produced major negative outcomes and only limited adaptation after setbacks.

contrary_evidence.explanation: Kherson withdrawal shows a severe failure to achieve key war aims by year-end.
Economic contraction reflects the material cost of the war decision and limits claims of competent stewardship.
Inflation and sanctions pressure further show the program hurt domestic performance.

judge.source_mix: Mostly Reuters and official Kremlin material, plus official economic data. The evidence is strong on command and negative outcomes, but less strong on independent internal deliberation.
judge.structured_prior_summary: No structured local priors were collected. The dossier is judgeable because the war program and its failures are explicitly documented.
judge.chapter_rationale: Putin's 2022 record is one of decisive command followed by strategic failure. He clearly defined the program, mobilized the state, annexed territory, and intensified war production. But by year-end the dossier also shows a contractive economy, severe inflation, battlefield reverses, and a forced retreat from Kherson. That combination does not justify a high competence score. It shows capacity to command and sustain conflict, but not effective advancement of the stated program to a durable successful end state.
judge.lower_anchor_rejected: A lower score would ignore the unmistakable command, mobilization, and war-management capacity visible in the dossier.
judge.higher_anchor_rejected: A higher score is not justified because the war program produced major reversals, economic contraction, and only reactive adaptation rather than durable success.

chapter_specific.value: The score reflects execution and program advancement, not moral judgment on the invasion or regime.

judge.reader_abstract:
Overall, Vladimir Putin's record on effectiveness in 2022 was assessed as poor, resulting in a score of 3 out of 10.

Evidence supporting a more favorable assessment includes the following: Putin authorized the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and said the goal was to demilitarise and 'denazify' Ukraine; and Putin announced partial mobilization, tied the war to defense of territorial integrity, and said Russia would use all available means, adding that the warning was not bluff.

Evidence weighing against a stronger assessment includes the following: Russia said it had completed its withdrawal from Kherson, a lightning-fast retreat of tens of thousands of troops that Reuters described as a major setback and the loss of the only regional capital Russia captured after the invasion; and Rosstat said Russia's economy contracted by 1.2% in 2022, and Reuters noted that Western sanctions followed Putin's decision to send troops into Ukraine.

Responsibility and evidentiary limits matter here: Direct and strong across the central war decisions. Unlike many dossiers, attribution is not the problem; the problem is that the program produced major negative outcomes and only limited adaptation after setbacks.

Taken together, I did not go higher because a higher score is not justified because the war program produced major reversals, economic contraction, and only reactive adaptation rather than durable success. I did not go lower because a lower score would ignore the unmistakable command, mobilization, and war-management capacity visible in the dossier.

Overall, Andrés Manuel López Obrador's record on nuclear and existential responsibility in 2022 was assessed as generally positive, with important limitations, resulting in a score of 6 out of 10.

judge.inherited_baseline_and_constraints: Mexico's severe crime and cartel environment complicate attribution; the score isolates AMLO-era federal choices, protection failures, and tolerated coercive trends rather than all local violence.
judge.ruler_attribution: Mixed: direct for federal policy proposals and transparency choices, indirect for many killings and intimidation events driven by local or criminal actors.

judge.source_mix: Rights NGOs, UN communications, official presidential material, and Reuters-style reporting; no client matrix used.
judge.structured_prior_summary: Structured local priors were unavailable across the lens set, so the score relies on the cited evidence and the dossier's embedded contrary notes.
judge.chapter_rationale: Mexico sits in the middle band because the dossier shows substantial domestic-safety failures, but not a single centralized terror system. The worst facts are repeated journalist killings, state-actor press abuse, surveillance, militarization, and serious obstruction around Ayotzinapa. The positive side is thin but real: the administration did pursue a truth commission and public transparency steps, which stops the score from falling further. Yet the year still reads as a dangerous mix of coercive state behavior, criminal violence, and weak remedy, so the chapter score remains clearly below a protective democracy but above the severe-authoritarian floor.

judge.reader_abstract:
Overall, Andrés Manuel López Obrador's record on domestic safety in 2022 was assessed as mixed, resulting in a score of 4 out of 10.

Evidence supporting a more favorable assessment includes the following: In 2022 Mexico recorded 696 attacks against the press, 12 journalists were murdered, 42.53% of documented attacks were perpetrated directly by state actors, and the executive branch made 176 stigmatizing comments against media, journalists, and civil society; and At least 13 journalists were killed in Mexico in the first eight months of 2022, the highest number CPJ had ever documented in the country in a single year; CPJ also noted that at least nine reporters and dozens of human rights defenders had been killed while technically under federal protection.

Evidence weighing against a stronger assessment includes the following: The presidency said AMLO's commitment was to tell the truth, that 41,168 documents had been reviewed, the report and annexes were public, three students had been identified, and there were sufficient elements to continue investigating 33 people; and The UN communication concerns the killings of Esmeralda Gallardo Sánchez and María del Carmen Vázquez, two women searchers, in a context of growing attacks against relatives and collectives searching for disappeared people in Mexico.

Responsibility and evidentiary limits matter here: Mixed: direct for federal policy proposals and transparency choices, indirect for many killings and intimidation events driven by local or criminal actors.

Taken together, I did not go higher because I rejected 5+ because repeated journalist killings, surveillance, and militarization are too serious to call the year broadly safe. I did not go lower because I rejected 2-3 because the file contains some real transparency and legal action, so it is not a purely collapsed remedy environment.

evidence.claim: The UN human-rights office said illicit surveillance against journalists and human-rights defenders constituted arbitrary interference, came to light through leaked Sedena documents or a government-acquired software package, and had an intimidating effect that signaled intolerance of criticism.

evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official UN human-rights statement issued contemporaneously in Mexico with direct normative assessment.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 evidence about the ruler-period information environment and state surveillance concerns.
evidence.ruler_attribution: The statement concerns state institutions under the AMLO government, but does not directly name the top-level order giver.
contrary_evidence: The UN note stops short of naming AMLO personally as the person who ordered surveillance.
It is a human-rights concern statement, not a court finding.

decisive_positive_evidence.explanation: The recall process and its official count show that a meaningful constitutional contestability mechanism remained live in 2022.
AMLO's own electoral-reform proposal can be read as a stated attempt to justify clean elections, though it was politically contested and not necessarily freedom-enhancing in effect.
His public denial of reelection intent matters because it directly addresses transfer-rule concerns, even if self-denial is not proof of compliance.

decisive_negative_evidence.explanation: ARTICLE 19's 2022 attack count, including state-actor involvement and stigmatizing executive comments, is strong evidence of a hostile media environment.
The UN human-rights statement on illicit surveillance against journalists and defenders shows state pressure on criticism.
Congress rejected AMLO's controversial electoral reform, which shows the executive sought rule changes that many saw as threatening independence even though the legislature blocked them.
The hostile morning briefing style singled out journalists and publications, which is a ruler-linked pressure pattern.
The 2022 press-attack totals and stigmatizing executive comments are strong evidence that political and media space was meaningfully degraded.
UN OHCHR concern about illegal surveillance reinforces that the pressure was not merely rhetorical.

judge.inherited_baseline_and_constraints: Mexico retained real electoral competition and a constitutional transfer framework, but the AMLO administration exerted heavy rhetorical and administrative pressure on media and critics. The system was open enough to resist his electoral reform, yet not free of executive intimidation.
judge.ruler_attribution: Mixed: some evidence is directly AMLO's own rhetoric and proposals, while other evidence shows state or surveillance behavior under his administration without a clean personal-order transcript.

contrary_evidence.explanation: The recall process shows that democratic contestability still functioned, preventing a lower authoritarian score.
Congress rejecting the reform shows institutional resistance, which moderates the score upward.

judge.source_mix: A mix of official election and presidential records, Reuters, ARTICLE 19, UN human-rights reporting, and media/journalism research. The evidence is broad and credible, though some of the strongest abuse claims are indirect or system-level rather than personally ordered.
judge.structured_prior_summary: Structured local priors were not collected in this experiment; the judge relied entirely on the embedded projection and its cited evidence.
judge.chapter_rationale: Andrés Manuel López Obrador's 2022 Mexico is a mixed democracy with real contestability but clear executive pressure. The recall process and legislative resistance show that the system could still constrain him, and he did not eliminate transfer rules. Yet the record also shows a hostile media environment, surveillance concerns, stigmatizing executive comments, and an attempted electoral reform that critics believed would weaken independence. That makes the score squarely midrange: not an authoritarian slide, but definitely not a clean freedom-preserving presidency.
judge.lower_anchor_rejected: A lower score would miss the fact that electoral contestability and legislative checks actually worked in 2022.
judge.higher_anchor_rejected: A higher score would ignore the scale of media hostility, surveillance concerns, and the attempted institutional redesign around elections.

chapter_specific.value: Mixed and mildly erosive: democratic institutions held, but executive rhetoric and pressure narrowed freedom.

judge.reader_abstract:
Overall, Andrés Manuel López Obrador's record on political freedom in 2022 was assessed as mixed, resulting in a score of 5.5 out of 10.

Evidence supporting a more favorable assessment includes the following: INE completed the 2022 recall count, reporting 17.77% participation and 91.86% for López Obrador to stay in office; the INE leadership described the day as a free, secret, peaceful civic exercise; and AMLO said his administration would send a constitutional electoral-reform proposal to Congress to guarantee clean and free elections and to leave behind electoral fraud.

Evidence weighing against a stronger assessment includes the following: In 2022 Mexico recorded 696 attacks against the press, 12 journalists were murdered, 42.53% of documented attacks were perpetrated directly by state actors, and the executive branch made 176 stigmatizing comments against media, journalists, and civil society; and UN human-rights staff said leaked Sedena documents or a government-acquired software package revealed illicit surveillance against journalists and human-rights defenders, calling it grave, intimidating, and contrary to a safe environment for criticism.

Responsibility and evidentiary limits matter here: Mixed: some evidence is directly AMLO's own rhetoric and proposals, while other evidence shows state or surveillance behavior under his administration without a clean personal-order transcript.

Taken together, I did not go higher because a higher score would ignore the scale of media hostility, surveillance concerns, and the attempted institutional redesign around elections. I did not go lower because a lower score would miss the fact that electoral contestability and legislative checks actually worked in 2022.

judge.inherited_baseline_and_constraints: Mexico in 2022 had a resilient macro framework, but weak long-run investment, energy-policy uncertainty, and ongoing poverty and health challenges. judge.ruler_attribution: Attribution is mixed: the poverty decline and labor outcomes support AMLO-era relevance, but the investment and energy weaknesses are also partly inherited and institutional.

judge.source_mix: OECD, World Bank, Reuters, official budget releases, and independent poverty analysis; no structured local priors were collected in this experiment.
judge.structured_prior_summary: Structured local priors were unavailable across all lenses; the judgment depends on the dossier evidence and source-confidence metadata only.
judge.chapter_rationale: AMLO scores 5.5 because Mexico showed real household progress in 2022, especially on poverty, while the government also used subsidies and fiscal management to cushion inflation. The ceiling is lower than a 7 because the energy and investment story is still troubling: policy uncertainty, weak enforcement, and concern about missing new industrial opportunities all remained visible. This is a mixed prosperity record with real social gains but persistent structural and investor-confidence weaknesses.
judge.lower_anchor_rejected: A score near 4.5 would understate the poverty reduction and household cushioning documented in the dossier.
judge.higher_anchor_rejected: A score near 6.5 would overstate the quality of the investment climate and the durability of the gains.

chapter_specific.value: Household welfare improved on poverty metrics, but the investment trajectory remained too uncertain for a high score.
Inflation and post-pandemic conditions mattered, but the energy-policy environment was also a meaningful self-inflicted constraint.
The poverty decline is the main positive; health access and long-run opportunity still lagged behind headline improvement.

judge.reader_abstract:
Overall, Andr�e9s Manuel L�f3pez Obrador's record on economic well-being in 2022 was assessed as mixed, resulting in a score of 5.5 out of 10.

Evidence supporting a more favorable assessment includes the following: The World Bank said Mexico's official multidimensional poverty rate fell from 43.2 percent in 2016 to 36.3 percent in 2022, lifting 5.4 million people out of poverty and noting that the improvement was driven mainly by labor-market outcomes, including minimum-wage increases; and Reuters reported that Mexico's anti-inflation subsidies cost about 575 billion pesos in 2022, with 430 billion pesos going to gasoline-price subsidies, and officials said the measures helped ease the pain of ordinary people.

Evidence weighing against a stronger assessment includes the following: Reuters reported that López Obrador's plan to increase state control of power generation was defeated in parliament after opposition parties said it would hurt investment and breach international obligations; and Reuters said Mexico risked missing an investment windfall from the semiconductor boom because firms were worried about power supply, fossil-fuel dependence, and weak incentives.

Responsibility and evidentiary limits matter here: Attribution is mixed: the poverty decline and labor outcomes support AMLO-era relevance, but the investment and energy weaknesses are also partly inherited and institutional.

Taken together, I did not go higher because a score near 6.5 would overstate the quality of the investment climate and the durability of the gains. I did not go lower because a score near 4.5 would understate the poverty reduction and household cushioning documented in the dossier.
